title: Short-term rental upsells that pay for themselves: what we learned from real host data
summary: We looked at every early check-in, late checkout, and add-on that hosts sold through ProhostAI. The best setups covered their whole software bill. One habit separated them from everyone else: they put the link in front of guests automatically.
body_markdown:
**Yes, upsells can pay for your software. ProhostAI hosts with a complete upgrade setup earn about $137 per listing per year from early check-ins, late checkouts and add-ons, and the top quarter earn about $250. For a 50-listing portfolio, that's roughly $7,000–12,500 a year. The difference between hosts who earn and hosts who don't is rarely the upgrade itself. It's whether guests ever see the link.**


Every host has had a guest ask "any chance we could check in early?" Most hosts answer in a chat thread, decide on the spot, and either give it away or don't charge at all. Across a portfolio, that's a lot of small decisions worth real money.


Since we launched paid upgrades, guests have bought early check-ins, late checkouts, pool heating, golf carts, pet fees, breakfast baskets and more through ProhostAI. We pulled every one of those purchases to answer three questions:


1. How much can a host realistically earn?
2. Which upgrades actually sell?
3. What do the top-earning hosts do differently?


## Key takeaways


- **About $137 per listing per year, $250 for the top quarter.** That's roughly **$3,400–6,300 a year for a 25-listing portfolio** and **$13,700–25,000 for 100 listings** .
- **Upgrades can cover the software.** Among hosts with a complete setup who have made sales, upgrade revenue covered **1.6×** their ProhostAI bill at 1–25 listings and about **1×** at 26+ listings.
- **Automation is the biggest lever.** Hosts who put the upgrade link in automated guest messages earn **~6× more per listing** than hosts who switched upgrades on and waited ($9.11 vs. $1.59 per listing per month).
- **Early check-in is half the money.** Early check-in is **53%** of upgrade revenue, late checkout **27%** , and add-ons the remaining **21%** .
- **Pricing off the nightly rate wins.** Early check-ins priced as a percentage of the nightly rate average **$120** , compared with **$30** for a flat fee.
- **Guests buy late.** **44%** of early check-ins are bought in the last 6 hours before arrival.
- **Hiding upgrades on same-day turnovers halves** the requests you end up declining (23% → 12%).


## 1. Upgrades can pay for your software


Start with what a listing earns. At hosts with a complete setup (payouts connected, upgrades on, and the link in automated guest messages), a listing with upgrades turned on brings in about **$11.40 a month, or $137 a year** . The top quarter of hosts earn about **$21 a month, or $250 a year** , per listing. Multiply that across a portfolio and it adds up quickly; the chart at the top of this post shows the estimate for portfolios of 5 to 300 listings.


Our customers ask about ROI all the time. For upgrades, the answer is easy to measure: compare what hosts earned from upgrades with what they paid us.


Upgrade revenue as a multiple of the ProhostAI bill, by portfolio size


For hosts with up to 25 listings, upgrades brought in **1.6×** their ProhostAI bill. Larger operators broke even on average. That's despite the fact that most of them still sell only early check-in and late checkout, and at only ~3% of stays.


The spread between hosts is wide:


Host Upgrade revenue per listing with upgrades on, per month


Median host (complete setup, already selling) ~$10


Top 25% of hosts $21+


Best performers (small portfolios, strong add-ons) $50–150


The best performers aren't in a different business from the median host. They made five or six setup choices the median host hasn't made yet. The rest of this post covers them.


## 2. Put the link in front of guests automatically


This was the single biggest difference in the data.


Some hosts switched upgrades on and stopped there. The upgrades sat in the guidebook, and guests found them only if they went looking. Other hosts added the guidebook or upgrade link to their automated guest messages: booking confirmation, pre-arrival, check-out instructions.


Upgrade revenue per listing per month, with and without the link in automated messages


Hosts who automated the link earned **$9.11 per listing per month** , compared with **$1.59** for hosts who didn't. **78%** of them made at least one sale, compared with **31%** of hosts who skipped this step.


What did *not* work as well: one-off sales pitches. The large majority of purchases came from guests browsing the upgrades in their guidebook, not from a standalone "want to check in early?" text. One pattern performed especially badly: offer messages that say "let me know if you're interested" with no way to pay. Guests don't reply to those; they buy when there's a button.


**What to do:**


- Put your guidebook link in at least three[automated messages](https://prohost.ai/scheduled-messages) :


- **Booking confirmation:** the guest is excited and planning.
- **2–3 days before arrival:** the guest is booking flights and wondering when they can get in.
- **Check-out instructions (the day before departure):** this is the late-checkout moment.


- Use a direct upgrade link for the specific moment. For example, add "Want to sleep in? Book a late checkout →" with the late-checkout link to your checkout message.
- If you send offer messages, every one should contain a link the guest can pay through.


## 3. What actually sells


Share of upgrade revenue by type


**Early check-in is the workhorse:** more than half of all upgrade revenue. Guests landing at 9am don't want to wander around with luggage until 4pm, and they'll happily pay to avoid it. **Late checkout** is about a quarter, mostly bought by guests with afternoon flights.


The remaining fifth comes from **add-ons** , and add-ons carry the biggest tickets. The best-selling add-ons we saw:


- **Pool and hot tub heating:** in season, this can run several hundred dollars per stay. It was the single highest-value upgrade in the data.
- **Golf carts, bikes and beach gear:** priced per day for the whole stay.
- **Pet fees:** guests would rather pay up front than sneak a dog in.
- **Breakfast and welcome baskets:** an easy add-on wherever there's a local bakery or farm.
- **Mid-stay cleaning and towel refresh:** an easy sell on stays of a week or more.
- **Pre-paid parking:** especially in cities.
- **Lost key and fob replacement:** not glamorous, but it collects a fee you'd otherwise chase by text.


**What to do:** Start with early check-in and late checkout on every listing, then add **2–5 add-ons that fit the property** . The top add-on sellers all had a **photo on every upgrade** and a description that explains exactly what the guest gets. Resist listing dozens of options: a short menu with photos is easier to buy from than a long list of text.


## 4. Price early check-in and late checkout off the nightly rate


How you price early check-in and late checkout changes what you earn more than almost anything else:


Average sale by pricing model for early check-in and late checkout


A flat $25–30 early check-in is the most common setup. It's also the cheapest. Pricing per hour roughly doubles the average sale. Pricing as a **percentage of that night's rate** (for example, 30% of the empty night before arrival) averages **$120 for early check-in and $98 for late checkout** .


Part of that gap is that percentage-based upgrades usually unlock a bigger window (up to a full day). That's the point, though: when the night before is empty anyway, a guest arriving at 10am is worth a meaningful share of that night, and they know it.


**What to do:** Use percentage-of-nightly-rate pricing when there's a gap night, and per-hour pricing for shorter windows on turnover days. Keep flat fees for small, fixed perks.


## 5. Guests buy at the last minute, so be there when they do


When guests buy early check-in and late checkout, relative to arrival and departure


**44% of early check-ins are bought in the 6 hours before arrival** , often from the airport. Late checkouts peak in the **6–24 hours before departure** , when the guest reads their check-out instructions.


That matters in two ways:


1. **Timing your messages.** A link sent only at booking misses the moment of need. The check-in-day message and the check-out-instructions message do the heavy lifting.
2. **Speed of approval.** A request at 8am for an 11am check-in is worthless if it's approved at 2pm. The typical host in our data approves in about 20 minutes, but the slowest tenth of requests waited **22 hours or more** , and some expired unanswered.


**What to do:**


- Turn on **auto-approve** for anything that doesn't depend on the calendar: pet fees, add-ons, parking.
- For early check-in and late checkout, keep approvals on your phone with push notifications, or let your AI assistant handle them when the calendar is clear.


## 6. Don't sell what you can't deliver


The fastest way to annoy a guest is to take their money for an early check-in and then refund it because the cleaners are still inside.


Share of early check-in and late checkout requests declined or expired, by same-day turnover setting


Hosts who offered early check-in and late checkout even on **same-day turnovers** (another guest leaving or arriving that day) ended up declining or letting expire **23%** of requests. Hosts who **hid those upgrades on turnover days** declined only **12%** . Every declined request is a disappointed guest and a refund to process.


**What to do:**


- Hide early check-in and late checkout on same-day turnovers by default.
- Let early check-in reopen automatically once the turnover clean is marked complete, so you still capture the days when your cleaners finish early.
- Set a **maximum per request** , so a guest can't stack two late checkouts.


## Your 15-minute upsell setup checklist


If you only do the essentials, do these. They're what the top-earning hosts in our data have in common.


1. **Connect payouts first.** Guests can't pay until your payout account is live.
2. **Turn on early check-in and late checkout for every listing.** Price them off the nightly rate or per hour, not a $25 flat fee.
3. **Hide them on same-day turnovers** , and let early check-in reopen when the clean is done.
4. **Add 2–5 add-ons that fit your properties** , each with a photo and a clear description.
5. **Put the link in three automated messages:** booking confirmation, 2–3 days before arrival, and check-out instructions.
6. **Use direct upgrade links** in the message where each upgrade matters most.
7. **Auto-approve add-ons** , and turn on push notifications for the rest.
8. **If owners should get the money** , set the payout recipient per upgrade so you're not reimbursing them by hand.


## The takeaway


Upsells aren't a nice-to-have bolted onto hosting. Done right, they're a revenue line that can pay for your whole software stack. The hosts winning at it aren't selling anything exotic: early check-in, late checkout and a few add-ons that suit the property. What sets them apart is that **guests see the link at the moment they need it, can pay in one tap, and get a fast yes.**
